understanding.does: You sell a post-quantum cryptographic verification layer to institutions and developers who need to verify transactions before settlement, without changing existing infrastructure.
understanding.standsOut: You are betting on being the dedicated verification layer that sits between intent and settlement across every existing network.

constraint.text: No institution has integrated QuFi and processed a real transaction through it yet.

evidence: No named customer, pilot result or live integration shown anywhere on the site.
Performance figures (10,000+ nodes, 100,000+ verifications per second, 99.99% uptime) are stated as targets and goals, not measured outcomes.
200+ organisations described as "in pipeline", not as signed or live.
QuVault, QuSettle and QuFi Verify have no pricing, no sign-up and no destination page behind their Explore links.

conversation:
BB: I have read what you gave me on QuFi Network. One thing stands out before we talk.
Your site sells the protocol's architecture in depth, but the three things a buyer could actually sign up for get one paragraph each and no way to start.
You have 200+ organisations in pipeline across 50+ countries, yet none are named and no result is shown: the credibility gap between that claim and the evidence on the site is wide.
You are 60 days from a testnet that a bank's security team can run against, which means the window to get the right first buyer into that test is right now, not after it ships.
Which of the three products is the one you are actually selling into that first bank engagement.
Which product is the real lead right now?

FOUNDER: The bank's security team will run an end-to-end verification of a real 
transaction flow: they submit a transaction, our node verifies it, and 
they receive a signed proof they can validate independently. If they 
can reproduce that on their own infrastructure without our engineers 
on the call, we've passed.

BB: That is a sharp, binary test: they either reproduce the proof without you, or they do not. What it tells me is that the product being evaluated is the core verification layer itself, not QuVault or QuSettle as packaged products. The bank is testing the engine, not the wrapper. That matters because it means your commercial model question is still open: if they pass the test, what do they actually sign? A node licence, an enterprise contract, a per-verification fee arrangement?

When the bank says yes after the test, what does the commercial agreement look like: do they pay per verification, licence a node, sign an enterprise contract, or something else entirely?

FOUNDER: API references exist. QPL onboarding is partial — a developer can read 
it but needs our team for the first setup. Environment setup is 
manual today. All three would need to be tightened before a bank's 
team can run solo. That's the real work of the next 60 days.

BB: Got it: the 60 days are not about the protocol being unready, they are about the handoff being unready. The bank can't run solo yet because the onboarding path still requires your engineers in the room. That is a different problem than a technical one, and it is actually the sharper risk: you could pass the cryptographic test and still fail the independence test because the setup friction keeps your team in the loop. One thing I still don't know, and it changes everything about what you are actually selling: when the bank passes the test and says yes, what does the commercial agreement look like? Do they pay per verification, licence a node, sign an enterprise contract, or something else?

When the bank says yes after the test, what does the commercial agreement look like: per verification, node licence, enterprise contract, or something else?

FOUNDER: Both. Two of the warm contacts are actively waiting for the testnet 
date — they've asked us twice. The rest are warm introductions that 
went quiet. The 60-day clock is real for the two active ones; for the 
rest, we need the testnet live before they re-engage.
